Such risk factors include: Lifestyle factors, such as smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, and a less healthy diet Major contact with cancer-causing chemicals, such as pesticides Health conditions, such as diabetes and chronic inflammation of the pancreas Close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary. This means that a higher risk was passed down to you by your parents through your genes. The genetic cause of hereditary pancreatic cancer is unknown in most families. Hereditary health conditions that are known to increase risk of pancreatic cancer include: Hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC) Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome Familial malignant melanoma syndrome, also known as melanoma-pancreatic cancer syndrome or familial atypical multiple mole melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome Hereditary pancreatitis Genetic tests detect the genes that have been linked to these hereditary conditions and are discussed in Chapter What are the stages of pancreatic cancer? The stages of pancreatic cancer range from stage 0 to stage Often, stages 1 through 4 are written with Roman numerals—stages I, II, III, and IV. The cancer stages are based on the size of the pancreatic tumor and how far the cancer has spread. Stage 0 pancreatic cancer is only in the innermost layer of the duct wall. Stage 1 pancreatic cancer consists of a tumor that is 4 centimeters or smaller and has not spread outside the pancreas. For comparison, a golf ball is 3 centimeters. h Stage 2 pancreatic cancer consists of a tumor that is larger than 4 centimeters or the cancer has spread to 1 to 3 nearby lymph nodes, which are small structures that help the body fight disease. Stage 3 pancreatic cancer has grown through the pancreas to nearby major arteries or has spread to 4 or more lymph nodes. Stage 4 pancreatic cancer has spread far and commonly involves the liver, lungs, or lining of the abdomen. What stage is metastatic cancer? Stage 4 pancreatic cancer is metastatic cancer, but other stages may become metastatic cancer over time. Metastatic pancreatic cancer has spread far from the pancreas. Is staging used to plan treatment for pancreatic cancer? Unlike other cancers, experts do not plan initial treatment mainly based on the five pancreatic cancer stages. Instead, they use a different system to decide treatment for cancers that are not metastatic. This system is described in Chapter What is the best treatment for pancreatic cancer? There’s no treatment for pancreatic cancer that’s best for everyone. The best treatment is the treatment that’s right for you. Your treatment plan should follow best practices— cancer care based on science and expert consensus. The following chapters explain the best practices of testing for and treating pancreatic cancer. Some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer have surgery to remove cancer from the body. Surgery is an option for more people now than in the past due to medical advances. Other types of cancer treatment are used with Pancreatic cancer stages Very rarely, pancreatic cancer is only in the duct (stage 0) or only in the pancreas (stage 1 or some stage 2). Stage 2 and stage 3 also include cancers that have spread to beanshaped structures called lymph nodes (shown). Other stage 3 cancers have grown to nearby arteries, such as the celiac axis. Most often, pancreatic cancer has spread far from the pancreas, which is stage surgery to improve results. Ongoing research is assessing whether it is better to receive these other treatments before or after surgery. Read Chapter 5 to learn more about treatment with surgery. For most people with pancreatic cancer, surgery is not the best treatment. Instead, drug treatment is most often used to control cancer’s growth and reduce symptoms. Research has compared current cancer drugs to identify the best ones. In recent years, drug regimens based on cancer markers have been used to improve results. Treatment without surgery is discussed in Chapter Clinical trials offer hope to all people with pancreatic cancer. Clinical trials are a type of health research that tests new ways of fighting cancer. Ask your care team if there is a clinical trial that is a good fit for you. Hormone therapies for prostate cancer include luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists and LHRH antagonists, both of which cause the testicles to stop making testosterone. You may have heard of leuprolide (Lupron), a commonly used LHRH agonist or degarelix (Firmagon), a commonly used LHRH antagonist. Most LHRH agonists and LHRH antagonists are injections. These may be given monthly, or 2, 3, or 4 times a year. The exception is relugolix (Orgovyx), an LHRH antagonist that comes as a tablet taken once a day. Anti-androgens, corticosteroids, and androgen synthesis inhibitors are also available as pills and taken 1 to 3 times a day, depending on the medication. See Guide Newer hormone therapies Hormone therapy has been the main treatment for advanced prostate cancer for several decades. Longstanding hormone therapies (such as bicalutamide, flutamide, and nilutamide) are sometimes still used for treating prostate cancer.
Breast cancer basics The breast Breast cancer How breast cancer spreads Key points Invasive breast cancer is cancer that has spread from the milk ducts or milk glands into the breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. The breast The breast is an organ and a gland found on the chest. The breast is made of milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. Behind the breast is the pectoral (chest) muscle and ribs. Muscle and ligaments help hold the breast in place. Breast tissue contains glands that can make milk. These milk glands are called lobules. Lobules look like tiny clusters of grapes. Small tubes called ducts connect the lobules to the nipple. The ring of darker breast skin is called the areola. The raised tip within the areola is called the nipple. The nipple-areola complex (NAC) is a term that refers to both parts. Lymph drains from breast tissue into lymph vessels and travels to lymph nodes near your armpit (axilla). Lymph is a clear fluid that gives cells water and food. It also helps to fight germs. Nodes near the armpit are called axillary lymph nodes (ALNs). The breast The breast is a glandular organ made up of milk ducts, fat, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. Breast cancer Breast cancer starts in the cells of the breast. Almost all breast cancers are a subtype called carcinomas. Carcinomas are cancers that start in the cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. There are different types of breast carcinoma, most of which arise in cells that make up the lining (epithelial cells) in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast. The most common types are either ductal or lobular. Anyone can develop breast cancer, including those assigned male at birth. Although there are some differences between those assigned male and those assigned female at birth, treatment is very similar for all genders. How breast cancer spreads Cancer cells don’t behave like normal cells. Cancer cells differ from normal cells in the following ways. Primary tumor Over time, cancer cells form a mass called a primary tumor. Invasive Cancer cells can grow into surrounding tissues. Invasive breast cancer is breast cancer that has spread from the milk ducts or milk glands (lobules) into the surrounding breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. Metastasis Unlike normal cells, cancer cells can spread and form tumors in other parts of the body called metastases. In this process, cancer cells break away from the first (primary) tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites. Once in other sites, cancer cells may form secondary tumors. Cancer that has spread to a nearby body part such as the axillary lymph nodes is called a local metastasis. It might be referred to as local/regional disease or locally advanced. Cancer that has spread to a body part far from the primary tumor is called a distant metastasis. Breast cancer can metastasize almost anywhere but most commonly spreads to the bone (including spine), lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. Breast cancer that has metastasized to other parts of the body is still called breast cancer. More information on metastatic breast cancer is available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Key points Anyone can develop breast cancer, but breast cancer occurs more frequently in persons assigned female at birth. Inside breasts are lobules, ducts, fat, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and connective tissue. Lobules are structures that make breast milk. Ducts carry breast milk from the lobules to the nipple. Breast cancer arises from epithelial cells (cells that make up the lining) in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast. Invasive breast cancer is cancer that has grown outside the ducts or lobules into surrounding tissue. Once outside the ducts or lobules, breast cancer can spread through lymph or blood to lymph nodes or other parts of the body. Metastatic breast cancer (MBC) has spread outside the breast and lymph nodes under the arm (axilla). Anyone can develop breast cancer, including those assigned male at birth. This book is organized into the following chapters: Chapter 2: Testing for ALL provides an overview of tests your child might receive, how fertility might be impacted by treatment, and the role of genetic and biomarker mutation testing. Chapter 3: Types of treatments gives a general overview of treatment. Everyone with ALL will be treated with steroids and multiagent chemotherapy. Other types of systemic therapy might be given. Chapter 4: Supportive care discusses what is supportive care and possible side effects of treatment. Chapter 5: BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL discusses treatment for the most common type of B-ALL. A clinical trial is the preferred treatment for these types of B-ALL. Chapter 6: BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL treatment aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL protein caused by the BCR::ABL1 gene. Treatment is usually an intensive combination of systemic therapies. Chapter 7: T-ALL discusses a group of cancers that start in T-cell lymphocytes. T-ALL is less common than B-ALL. Treatment options include a clinical trial or chemotherapy. Chapter 8: Infant ALL treatment is different than for other age groups. Infants are those under 12 months of age. Chapter 9: Other resources provides information on patient advocacy groups and where to get help. What can you do to get the best care? Advocate for your child and yourself. You have an important role to play in their care. In fact, you’re more likely to get the care you want by asking questions and making shared decisions with the care team. Consider seeking the opinion of an ALL specialist and treatment at an experienced children’s (pediatric) leukemia center. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients will help you understand cancer care. With better understanding, you’ll be more prepared to discuss care with your child's team and share your concerns. Many people feel more satisfied when they play an active role in their care. You may not know what to ask the care team. That’s common. Each chapter in this book ends with an important section called Questions to ask. These suggested questions will help you get more information on all aspects of care. Pancreatic cancer basics What is pancreatic cancer? What causes pancreatic cancer? What are the stages of pancreatic cancer? What is the best treatment for pancreatic cancer? Key points Pancreatic cancer is one of the most common cancers. It is a challenging cancer to treat, but treatment is improving. Experts are studying the best ways to treat pancreatic cancer and are developing new treatments. Read this chapter to learn the answers to some common questions about pancreatic cancer. What is pancreatic cancer? Pancreatic cancer starts in a large gland called the pancreas. The pancreas is part of the digestive system. It makes enzymes that break down proteins, fats, sugars, and starches in food. It also makes hormones called insulin and glucagon that control blood sugar levels. Pancreatic cancer affects cell growth. Pancreatic cancer cells make many new cancer cells and do not die when they should. The overgrowth of pancreatic cancer cells becomes a mass called a tumor. Pancreatic cancer cells also don’t stay in place and may grow into nearby body tissue. They may break away from a tumor, spread to other areas, and form more tumors. There are 2 main types of pancreatic cancer The more common type of pancreatic cancer forms from exocrine cells. Exocrine cells make and move digestive enzymes. Pancreatic adenocarcinomas form from exocrine cells that line the tube-like ducts of the pancreas. They are also called pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and are the focus of this book. Pancreas Sounds like PAN-kree-us. The pancreas is deep inside the body. It sits just below the liver and behind the stomach. In adults, the pancreas is about 6 inches long. Less often, pancreatic cancer forms from endocrine cells. Endocrine cells make hormones. Pancreatic cancer that forms from endocrine cells is called a neuroendocrine tumor. Information on pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors can be found at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the app NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer. What causes pancreatic cancer? Many people with cancer wonder how they got it. Experts don’t know exactly what causes pancreatic cells to become cancer cells. But they do know several factors that increase the chance of developing pancreatic cancer. Such risk factors include: Lifestyle factors, such as smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, and a less healthy diet Major contact with cancer-causing chemicals, such as pesticides Health conditions, such as diabetes and chronic inflammation of the pancreas Close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary. with ovarian cancer. It can determine if you have a mutation in the BRCA genes, or in other genes that play a role in hereditary cancer. Nutritional and digestive tract health Your provider may ask about your diet and eating habits. Symptoms of ovarian cancer include bloating, pain in the pelvis or abdomen, difficulty eating, and feeling full quickly. These symptoms may cause you to eat less in general, or to eat foods lacking in nutrients. Your overall health and nutrition level can have an impact on the success of surgery and other treatment outcomes. If you need help planning healthy meals or have questions about your diet, ask your provider for a referral to a registered dietitian or nutritionist. Your doctor may want to check your gastrointestinal (GI) tract using an imaging test. The GI tract is made of the organs that food passes through when you eat. This includes your stomach, small bowel, and large bowel (rectum and colon). An imaging tool called a scope is used to examine these organs. A scope is a long, thin tube with a light and a camera that can be guided into your body. A colonoscopy is used to examine the large bowel. This involves inserting a scope into your anus and guiding it through the rectum and colon. To examine the upper GI tract, a scope is guided down the throat into the esophagus, stomach, and small bowel. This is called an upper endoscopy. Blood tests The following tests are not used alone to diagnose ovarian cancer, but abnormal results may signal health problems. General health A complete blood count (CBC) measures the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in a sample of blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen throughout the body. White blood cells fight infection. Platelets help to control bleeding. Your blood counts may be too low or too high because of cancer or other health problems. A blood chemistry profile measures the levels of different chemicals that are affected by your kidneys, bones, and other organs and tissues. Levels that are too high or too low may be a sign that an organ isn’t working well. Abnormal levels may also be caused by the spread of cancer or by other diseases. This test can also provide information about nutrient intake, such as protein levels. This can help guide treatment decisions. The liver is an organ that does many important jobs, such as removing toxins from your blood. Liver function tests measure chemicals that are made or processed by the liver. Levels that are too high or low may be a sign of liver damage or cancer spread. Tumor markers A tumor marker is a substance found in body tissue or fluid that may be a sign of cancer. Along with other information, tumor markers can help diagnose ovarian cancer and monitor response to treatment. A cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) test is the most common tumor marker test for ovarian cancer. High levels of this protein in the blood may be a sign of ovarian or other cancers. A CA-125 test alone cannot diagnose ovarian cancer. Health problems that are not cancer, such as endometriosis and diverticulitis, can raise your CA-125 level. Some ovarian cancers don’t cause CA-125 to rise. Your blood may also be tested for the following tumor markers. These may be found in higherthan-normal amounts in people with less common ovarian cancers (LCOCs). Inhibin (typically inhibin A and inhibin B) Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) CA 19-9 HE4 Biomarker testing Biomarkers are features of the tumor that can help guide your treatment. They are often mutations (changes) in the DNA of the cancer cells. Testing for biomarkers involves analyzing a piece of tumor tissue in a lab or testing a sample of blood. The results can be used to determine whether you can join certain clinical trials, and whether you may benefit from specific maintenance therapies. Other names for biomarker testing include molecular testing, tumor profiling, genomic testing, tumor gene testing, next-generation sequencing (NGS), mutation testing, liquid biopsy, and precision oncology. BRCA and HRD A BRCA mutation is the most important biomarker used to plan ovarian cancer treatment. Everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer should have the tumor tested for mutations in the BRCA genes, and in other similar genes important in DNA repair. This is different than genetic testing of the blood for inherited (germline) BRCA mutations. Mutations in the tumor itself are known as somatic or simply “tumor” mutations. BRCA mutations are a form of homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). This means that if you have a BRCA mutation, the cancer is also homologous recombination deficient or HRD positive. However, you can also have an HRD-positive tumor without a BRCA mutation. Other changes in the tumor’s DNA can make it homologous recombination deficient. The tumor's BRCA and HRD status are used to guide decisions about maintenance therapy after initial treatment. Other biomarkers The timing of testing for the biomarkers described next can vary. Some providers test for these (in addition to BRCA) early in the treatment process. Others may only test for BRCA and wait to see if therapies that require other biomarkers are needed. However, testing for these biomarkers is generally recommended for ovarian cancer that returns after treatment (recurrent). Testing is performed on removed tumor tissue. Microsatellite instability (MSI) Mismatch repair (MMR) HER2 expression Tumor mutational burden (TMB) BRAF V600E mutation Folate receptor alpha (FRα) expression RET mutations NTRK gene fusion Key points The biopsy to diagnose ovarian cancer is usually done during initial surgery. Imaging is key to staging the cancer and deciding if surgery is a treatment option. Testing can also show if the cancer has unique features for which there is specific treatment. Multidisciplinary consult There is no tell-tale sign of pancreatic cancer, especially in early stages. Signs of pancreatic cancer may also be caused by other health conditions. Health care providers may suspect pancreatic cancer based on symptoms, such as yellowed skin or eyes called jaundice. Signs of pancreatic cancer on x-rays include widerthan-normal pancreatic ducts or an inflamed pancreas. If your provider suspects pancreatic cancer, testing will be needed. Care team Because pancreatic cancer is complex, it takes a team of experts to decide the best course to diagnose and treat pancreatic cancer. This team of experts should: Be multidisciplinary – Consist of health care providers from different fields of medicine Work at a high-volume center – Be very experienced with pancreatic cancer Care team A care team may include many multidisciplinary members, including a: Diagnostic radiologist Interventional radiologist Pathologist Gastroenterologist Medical oncologist Surgical oncologist Radiation oncologist Geriatrician Registered dietitian Genetic counselor Palliative care provider Mental health provider Many of these experts are supported by nurses, technicians, or assistants who are often on the frontline of cancer care. Look for descriptions of team members throughout this book. Consult meeting When your care team meets to consult with one another, they will review your health records and the tests done prior to your visit. Expect to be asked questions about your past and current health. This is called a medical history. You will also be asked about the health history of your close blood relatives. A team member will perform a physical exam of your body to check for signs of disease and to assess your physical ability. You will likely have at least one imaging scan and some of the other tests listed in Guide The team will discuss the diagnosis with you and if you need more tests. They will also discuss your treatment options. One of the main goals of the team is to decide if surgery is an option. The team will work with you to make a care plan that is specific to you. Stay positive, seek happiness and joy, surround yourself with love, and connect to a higher power."
Prostate cancer basics What is prostate cancer? What are the symptoms of prostate cancer? What causes prostate cancer? What is early-stage prostate cancer? Can prostate cancer be cured? Key points The prostate is a gland located deep inside the pelvis. Everyone with a prostate has a chance of getting prostate cancer. It’s usually not fatal, particularly early-stage prostate cancer. This chapter gives an overview of this common cancer. What is prostate cancer? Prostate cancer is a disease where cells in the prostate gland grow out of control. The prostate is a gland located just below the bladder in the pelvis, deep inside the area of your body between your hip bones. The prostate is about the size of a ping-pong ball and is an important part of the male reproductive system. Besides the prostate, the male reproductive system includes the penis, seminal vesicles, and testicles. Cancer is what happens when something goes wrong with the natural cell process causing some cells to grow out of control. Cancer cells don’t behave like normal cells. Cancer cells develop genetic changes (mutations) that allow them to multiply and make many more cancer cells. The cancer cells crowd out and overpower normal cells. This can end up harming the body. Cancer cells survive much longer than normal cells do. They can replace many normal cells and cause organs to stop working well. Cancer cells can also spread outside the prostate to other areas of the body. The prostate gland is an important part of the male reproductive system. It’s located in the pelvis just below the bladder and is about the size of a ping-pong ball. What are the symptoms of prostate cancer? A symptom is a feeling or problem that can indicate a disease or condition. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and shows no symptoms for a long time. But you don’t have to have symptoms to have prostate cancer. In fact, most patients who are diagnosed with early prostate cancer have no symptoms. Symptoms are more common for those with advanced prostate cancer. Symptoms, if they occur, can include: Blood in the urine or semen Burning or pain while urinating Unexplained weight loss Bone, hip, or back pain It’s important to know that prostate cancer has many of the same symptoms as a condition called enlarged prostate (also called benign prostatic hyperplasia, or BPH). An enlarged prostate can push against the bladder and compress the urethra, which slows the flow of urine and can cause a feeling that you haven’t fully emptied your bladder. Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in American males, after skin cancer. However, prostate cancer has one of the highest survival rates of any cancer when found early. BPH is much more common than prostate cancer. It’s difficult to tell the difference between the two conditions based on symptoms alone. Be sure to tell your health care providers if you have any of these symptoms: Urinating frequently, especially at night Weak or intermittent urine stream Trouble urinating or straining to urinate Trouble holding in urine Feeling like your bladder hasn’t fully emptied Dull pain in your groin or pelvis Erectile dysfunction (difficulty getting an erection) or painful ejaculation Where does the prostate fit in? A tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of tissue that arises from the uncontrolled overgrowth of cells, and it can be either benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). In the context of cancer, a tumor specifically refers to the primary cancerous mass, which is a key element in staging and treatment planning. Tumors can develop in various parts of the body, including lymph nodes, the prostate, the bladder, bones, the throat, and the ovaries, where they may present as solid or fluid-filled masses. Their size is often measured in centimeters or millimeters, and this measurement, along with the extent of local invasion into nearby structures, is used to assign a T score in cancer staging systems. For example, primary bone tumors are staged based on size and location, while throat and bladder tumors are assessed for their potential to invade deeper tissue layers or spread. Tumors may be detected as irregular or hardened areas during physical examination, such as in the prostate, or identified through medical procedures. Biopsy samples are commonly taken from tumors to determine whether they are cancerous, and in many cases, tumors can be surgically removed. Overall, the term tumor encompasses a wide range of abnormal growths, with its clinical significance largely determined by its benign or malignant nature, size, location, and potential for invasion or metastasis.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are a comprehensive set of patient-friendly guidelines published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), a nonprofit alliance of leading cancer centers. These guidelines translate the expert consensus of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into plain-language explanations, designed to help people with cancer, their families, and caregivers understand current care recommendations. The guidelines are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers, providing trusted, up-to-date information on cancer treatment, testing, staging, and side effects.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. They also address specific concerns such as immunotherapy side effects and fertility and family planning for cancer patients. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

The oropharynx is a part of the throat located behind the mouth, forming the middle section of the pharynx. It includes the back of the roof of the mouth (soft palate), the tonsils, the side and back walls of the throat, and the base of the tongue. In some clinical contexts, it is simply referred to as "the throat." This anatomical region is not fully visible when the mouth is opened, so examination typically requires special tools, such as during a procedure called panendoscopy.

The oropharynx is clinically significant in several diseases. For instance, p16-negative throat cancer originates in this area. Additionally, in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, the tumor may grow into the oropharynx at the T1 stage, and nasopharyngeal cancer can spread to this region. As a key part of the upper aerodigestive tract, the oropharynx serves as a critical site for both diagnostic evaluation and understanding the progression of head and neck cancers.

A tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of tissue that arises from the uncontrolled overgrowth of cells, and it can be either benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). In the context of cancer, a tumor specifically refers to the primary cancerous mass, which is a key element in staging and treatment planning. Tumors can develop in various parts of the body, including lymph nodes, the prostate, the bladder, bones, the throat, and the ovaries, where they may present as solid or fluid-filled masses. Their size is often measured in centimeters or millimeters, and this measurement, along with the extent of local invasion into nearby structures, is used to assign a T score in cancer staging systems. For example, primary bone tumors are staged based on size and location, while throat and bladder tumors are assessed for their potential to invade deeper tissue layers or spread. Tumors may be detected as irregular or hardened areas during physical examination, such as in the prostate, or identified through medical procedures. Biopsy samples are commonly taken from tumors to determine whether they are cancerous, and in many cases, tumors can be surgically removed. Overall, the term tumor encompasses a wide range of abnormal growths, with its clinical significance largely determined by its benign or malignant nature, size, location, and potential for invasion or metastasis.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.

Pathologic Stage, also known as surgical stage or pathologic stage (p), is the stage of cancer determined by examining tissue removed during a surgical procedure. This assessment is performed after the surgery has taken place, distinguishing it from clinical staging, which is based on examinations conducted before treatment. The pathologic stage is widely regarded as providing the most accurate picture of the disease's extent, as it is based on direct analysis of the actual removed tissue rather than imaging or physical exams alone.

This staging method offers more precise and detailed information regarding key prognostic factors, particularly the size of the primary tumor and the status of lymph nodes. By evaluating the tissue excised during operations such as lymph node removal, physicians can determine the exact degree of cancer spread. Consequently, the pathologic stage serves as a critical prognostic stage, informing treatment decisions and providing a more reliable basis for predicting patient outcomes than other staging methods.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.

CT Scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a medical imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles and combining them with a computer to produce detailed three-dimensional (3-D) pictures, as well as cross-sectional images of tissues, organs, and other structures. These scans are often performed with the use of a contrast agent to enhance image clarity, particularly for cancer detection and evaluation.

CT scans are widely used in oncology for detecting tumors, identifying cancer spread (metastasis), and staging diseases. They are commonly employed to image the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to check if cancer has spread to organs such as the liver, lungs, or other areas. For specific conditions, such as rectal cancer, CT scans help assess spread to chest and abdominal organs, while in colon cancer, they are used for surveillance in stages 2 and 3. Additionally, CT imaging is useful for detecting cancer spread to lymph nodes and for guiding procedures like lymph node or other biopsies.

Beyond diagnostic and staging purposes, CT scans play a critical role in treatment planning. A symptom is a problem or feeling that may signal a disease or condition. The most common symptom of bladder cancer, and the one that usually appears first, is having blood in your urine (hematuria). How does blood get into urine? Bladder tumors are likely to release a little blood, which mixes with the urine in your bladder. The blood may turn your urine pink or bright red. Or, if there isn’t enough blood to be visible, your urine may look normal. But your clinical team can still detect blood by looking at a sample of the urine under a microscope. Blood in the urine can be caused by many other things besides bladder cancer. The most common cause is an infection in the urinary tract. So anyone with blood in their urine should see a health care provider to get their urine tested. Other symptoms of bladder cancer include: Frequent urination Urgency to urinate Painful urination Back pain Not every person with bladder cancer will have all these symptoms. Some people will have no symptoms. A person with one or more of these symptoms should visit a doctor or other health care provider who can recommend different tests. These tests are used to make a diagnosis. (A diagnosis means identifying an illness by using tests.) What does aggressive mean? Bladder cancer When health care professionals describe cancer as aggressive, they mean the cancer is likely to grow or spread more quickly than average. Bladder cancer is often described by how far it has spread into the muscle layer of the bladder. Here, the cancer tumor has grown through the inner lining (urothelial layer) and invaded the muscle layer in the bladder wall. This type of cancer is known as muscleinvasive bladder cancer. Aggressive can also be used to describe a treatment that’s stronger or more intense than other treatment options. Genes are tiny parts of a cell that carry the instructions for how cells behave. These instructions also control how new cells are made. Sometimes, mutations can mix up these instructions. This can turn normal cells into cancer cells. In most people with bladder cancer, these mutations aren’t passed down in families (hereditary mutation). A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause bladder cancer. But people with bladder cancer often have one or more of these risk factors: Smoking – Smoking is the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. It accounts for about half of all cases. Their primary function is to filter blood, removing waste products and excess water to produce urine, which then drains through the ureters and, in some cases, a urinary diversion. Beyond filtration, the kidneys also produce hormones and are part of the broader urothelial lining. In medical imaging, the kidneys normally appear bright on PET scans and are involved in the excretion of contrast materials. Their function is a critical consideration in the use of contrast agents, as poor or impaired kidney function may preclude the administration of contrast material. Kidney function is routinely assessed through blood tests, including a chemistry profile or a comprehensive metabolic panel. Additionally, the kidneys are vulnerable to damage from certain treatments, such as high-dose methotrexate, which can potentially lead to kidney failure. The kidneys are examined through various procedures, including ureteroscopy and imaging techniques, to evaluate their structure and function.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

White Blood Cells, also known as leukocytes, are the infection-fighting cells of the blood and a crucial component of the immune system. They are primarily responsible for defending the body against infectious diseases and foreign germs. These cells are derived from blood stem cells and are found circulating in the bloodstream as well as within the lymphatic system, where they act as infection-fighting cells in the lymph.

White blood cells are categorized into several main types, including granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are a specific and vital subtype of white blood cell. Their concentration in the blood is a key health indicator, commonly measured as part of a Complete Blood Count (CBC) test.

The behavior and counts of white blood cells are clinically significant in various diseases. For instance, Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) originates in these cells, specifically in lymphocytes. Conversely, in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), white blood cell counts are often found to be abnormally high.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. What is pancreatic cancer? Pancreatic cancer starts in a large gland called the pancreas. The pancreas is part of the digestive system. It makes enzymes that break down proteins, fats, sugars, and starches in food. It also makes hormones called insulin and glucagon that control blood sugar levels. Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Pathologic Stage, also known as surgical stage or pathologic stage (p), is the stage of cancer determined by examining tissue removed during a surgical procedure. This assessment is performed after the surgery has taken place, distinguishing it from clinical staging, which is based on examinations conducted before treatment. The pathologic stage is widely regarded as providing the most accurate picture of the disease's extent, as it is based on direct analysis of the actual removed tissue rather than imaging or physical exams alone.

This staging method offers more precise and detailed information regarding key prognostic factors, particularly the size of the primary tumor and the status of lymph nodes. By evaluating the tissue excised during operations such as lymph node removal, physicians can determine the exact degree of cancer spread. Consequently, the pathologic stage serves as a critical prognostic stage, informing treatment decisions and providing a more reliable basis for predicting patient outcomes than other staging methods.

The prostate is a gland located just below the bladder in the pelvis, deep inside the area of your body between your hip bones. The prostate is an important part of the male reproductive system. Besides the prostate, the male reproductive system includes the penis, seminal vesicles, and testicles. Prostate cancer is one of the most common types of cancer. Cancer is what happens when something goes wrong with the natural cell process, which causes some cells to grow out of control. Cancer cells don’t behave like normal cells. Cancer cells develop genetic changes (mutations) that allow them to multiply and make many more cancer cells. The cancer cells crowd out and overwhelm normal cells. This can end up harming the body. Cancer cells can survive much longer than normal cells do. They can replace many normal cells and cause organs to stop working well. Cancer cells can also spread outside the prostate to other areas of the body. The prostate gland is an important part of the male reproductive system. It’s located in the pelvis just below the bladder and is typically about the size of a pingpong ball. What are the symptoms of prostate cancer? A symptom is a feeling or problem that can indicate a disease or condition. Prostate cancer often grows slowly and shows no symptoms for a long time. You don’t have to have symptoms to have prostate cancer. An enlarged prostate can push against the bladder and compress the urethra, which slows the flow of urine and can cause a feeling that you haven’t fully emptied your bladder. BPH is much more common than prostate cancer. It’s difficult to tell the difference between the two conditions based on symptoms alone. A risk factor is anything that increases your chance of getting cancer. Prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in those aged 65 years and above. Your chances of getting prostate cancer increase as you become older. The prostate also contains muscles that help propel semen through the urethra during ejaculation. Semen: A fluid made up of liquids from the prostate and the seminal vesicles as well as sperm from the testicles. During ejaculation, semen is released from the body through the urethra and out through the penis. Urethra: A tube that carries urine from the bladder and out of the body. The prostate surrounds the urethra just beneath the bladder. Seminal vesicles: Two glands that make and store another part of the fluid that becomes semen. Lynch Syndrome is a hereditary condition caused by mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes, which leads to a deficiency in DNA repair mechanisms. This inherited syndrome is the most common cause of hereditary colon and uterine (endometrial) cancers, and it significantly increases the risk of developing colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Beyond these primary sites, Lynch Syndrome is also associated with an elevated risk for other malignancies, including pancreatic cancer, adrenal tumors, and cancers of the urinary tract, such as bladder cancer. The condition is recognized as a key factor in clinical decision-making, particularly when considering germline testing for individuals with a personal or family history suggestive of these cancers. A tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of tissue that arises from the uncontrolled overgrowth of cells, and it can be either benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). In the context of cancer, a tumor specifically refers to the primary cancerous mass, which is a key element in staging and treatment planning. Tumors can develop in various parts of the body, including lymph nodes, the prostate, the bladder, bones, the throat, and the ovaries, where they may present as solid or fluid-filled masses. Their size is often measured in centimeters or millimeters, and this measurement, along with the extent of local invasion into nearby structures, is used to assign a T score in cancer staging systems. For example, primary bone tumors are staged based on size and location, while throat and bladder tumors are assessed for their potential to invade deeper tissue layers or spread. Tumors may be detected as irregular or hardened areas during physical examination, such as in the prostate, or identified through medical procedures. Biopsy samples are commonly taken from tumors to determine whether they are cancerous, and in many cases, tumors can be surgically removed. Overall, the term tumor encompasses a wide range of abnormal growths, with its clinical significance largely determined by its benign or malignant nature, size, location, and potential for invasion or metastasis.

Targeted Therapy is a form of systemic cancer treatment that uses medicines or drugs to identify and attack specific molecules, genes, proteins, or receptors involved in the growth, spread, and survival of cancer cells. Unlike broad-spectrum treatments like chemotherapy, this approach focuses on particular genetic changes, mutations (e.g., PIK3CA), or biomarkers (e.g., PARP inhibitors) present in tumors, making it effective for cancers with certain molecular features. By targeting these specific parts of cancer cells, the therapy aims to slow or stop tumor progression, and it may potentially cause fewer side effects than chemotherapy, though it can also be combined with chemotherapy in certain contexts, such as for primary CNS lymphoma.

This therapy is applicable across various cancer types, including advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent and/or metastatic cervical cancer, and thyroid cancers that cannot be treated with surgery or radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy, have recurred, or have metastasized and continue to grow. For thyroid cancer, the targeted therapies currently used are kinase inhibitors, typically administered as swallowed capsules. However, the treatment is not without risks; side effects can include body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding, and some agents may adversely affect the heart, skin, and digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can impact fertility, and its use is often guided by biomarker testing to determine patient eligibility.

As a systemic therapy, it is generally reserved for cases where specific genetic targets are identified, and it may be employed when other treatments have failed or are unsuitable. The overarching goal remains to attack specific types of cancer cells while minimizing harm to normal cells, thereby offering a more precise treatment option for individuals with particular gene mutations or molecular profiles.

Biomarker Testing is a medical procedure used in oncology that analyzes biological molecules—such as DNA mutations, proteins, or other molecular features—found in tumor tissue, biopsy samples, or blood to inform cancer care. Also known as molecular testing or tumor profiling, it is performed to identify specific genetic alterations or protein expressions that indicate the presence or progression of cancer, thereby aiding in diagnosis and prognosis. The testing examines genes or their products to detect mutations and proteins that may suggest effective treatment options, helping to guide decisions on whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies or immunotherapies.

The scope of biomarker testing is broad, encompassing various cancer types and specific markers. For instance, it is used to guide diagnosis and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and to assess risk and aggressiveness in prostate cancer by examining molecular components of biopsy samples. Common biomarkers tested include hormone receptors, HER2, PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, RET, p16, and EBV DNA, among others. These tests help determine the presence of specific biological markers that can predict response to particular drugs, thereby fine-tuning treatment plans and improving diagnostic accuracy.

Biomarker testing can be performed on tumor tissue or through liquid biopsies of blood, depending on the clinical need. The results provide critical information on the molecular profile of the cancer, enabling healthcare providers to select the most appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach. By identifying actionable mutations or protein levels, this testing plays a central role in precision medicine, ensuring that patients receive treatments most likely to be effective while avoiding unnecessary interventions.

It’s a procedure that removes tumors through the urethra without having to cut into the abdomen. The tumor can then be tested to provide a more detailed diagnosis. TURBT is done in an operating room in a clinic or hospital. You’ll be given anesthesia to put you to sleep. Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Chemoradiation is a treatment strategy that combines chemotherapy and radiation therapy, typically administered concurrently to enhance therapeutic efficacy. This approach is utilized across a range of cancer types, particularly for locally advanced or non-metastatic diseases. In the context of locally advanced cervical cancer, chemoradiation is recommended for most cases and involves the concurrent use of external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) alongside chemotherapy, often with a platinum-based regimen. Similarly, for most non-metastatic anal cancers and perianal cancers that do not meet criteria for local excision, chemoradiation is the standard recommended treatment. It is also employed in the management of bladder cancer, where chemotherapy and radiation therapy are used together. In cases of metastatic anal cancer, chemoradiation may be administered after initial chemotherapy, though it is not generally considered following a modified DCF (docetaxel, cisplatin, and fluorouracil) regimen. The treatment is broadly defined as the combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy, with specific applications varying by cancer type and stage. For anal cancer, clinical discussions often include considerations of chemotherapy regimens and radiation therapy details. Overall, chemoradiation serves as a cornerstone in the multidisciplinary management of several malignancies, aiming to improve local control and overall outcomes.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

The specific cause of CLL isn't currently known other than that there is a change within the bone marrow. It can be tied to several factors: Older adults tend to develop changes or mutations that could cause cancer like CLL to form over time Blood relatives of someone with CLL can have a higher chance of getting CLL themselves Lymph system Many B cells are in the lymph (or lymphatic) system. This system plays a key role in fighting infections. The tonsils, thymus, spleen, and lymph vessels and nodes are parts of the lymph system (shown). There are hundreds of lymph nodes in the body, and many are in the neck, armpits, and groin. How is CLL treated? Treatment of CLL depends on your body. You may not need treatment right away. But treatment may be needed if your white blood cell count is rising rapidly, if you have low numbers of other normal blood cells (anemia, low platelets, or low neutrophils), if you have large or uncomfortable lymph nodes, or if you have symptoms listed above. Many treatment options are available and should be discussed with your doctor at your first visit and as your condition is followed. These range from pills you take every day to a combination of IV infusions and pills taken for a specific amount of time. You may live for years without needing treatment. If or when someone needs treatment can vary greatly from person to person. You may have a more intense or aggressive treatment plan if you develop Richter transformation, which is described later. This rare condition can lead to a more aggressive cancer called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or another cancer called Hodgkin lymphoma. Is there a cure for CLL? There is currently no cure for CLL, but you can get effective treatment so your blood cells will be mostly healthy ones and a full life is possible. This is a condition called minimal residual disease. We’ll describe this in a later chapter. While the goal of treatment is not to cure CLL, the goal is to prevent the disease from causing problems and from becoming life-threatening. What is SLL? Small lymphocytic lymphoma, or SLL, is the same cancer as CLL. The only difference between the two is where the abnormal cells are found. CLL is mostly found in the blood and bone marrow. SLL is mostly found in lymph nodes and the spleen. If a person has fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells in their blood, it is considered SLL. Anything more than that is considered CLL. CT Scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a medical imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles and combining them with a computer to produce detailed three-dimensional (3-D) pictures, as well as cross-sectional images of tissues, organs, and other structures. These scans are often performed with the use of a contrast agent to enhance image clarity, particularly for cancer detection and evaluation.

CT scans are widely used in oncology for detecting tumors, identifying cancer spread (metastasis), and staging diseases. They are commonly employed to image the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to check if cancer has spread to organs such as the liver, lungs, or other areas. For specific conditions, such as rectal cancer, CT scans help assess spread to chest and abdominal organs, while in colon cancer, they are used for surveillance in stages 2 and 3. Additionally, CT imaging is useful for detecting cancer spread to lymph nodes and for guiding procedures like lymph node or other biopsies.

Beyond diagnostic and staging purposes, CT scans play a critical role in treatment planning. They are used during radiation therapy simulation to obtain precise pictures of the cancer site, which aids in creating an effective treatment plan. The technique is also considered an alternative imaging method when MRI is unavailable or not recommended, as CT scans are generally faster to perform than MRI scans. Overall, CT scans are a versatile and essential tool for diagnosing abnormalities, guiding interventions, and monitoring treatment outcomes.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Adenocarcinoma is a broad category of cancer that originates in glandular cells, which are responsible for producing and secreting substances such as mucus. This cancer type can arise in various organs, and its characteristics and prevalence differ depending on the location. In the lungs, adenocarcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that begins in the mucus-making cells lining the alveoli. It is the most common subtype of NSCLC. In the colorectal region, adenocarcinoma is the most frequent type of tumor, forming within adenomas (precancerous polyps) and representing the most common form of both colon and rectal cancer. It also accounts for the vast majority of colorectal cancers overall, distinguishing it from cancers arising from squamous cells.

Adenocarcinoma also occurs in other parts of the digestive and reproductive systems. In the stomach, it is the most common type of cancer, developing from the mucus-secreting cells that line the stomach wall; indeed, nearly all stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas. In the cervix, adenocarcinoma is a recognized type of cervical cancer that arises from the glandular cells located in the endocervix, and it is considered a common form of this disease. Additionally, adenocarcinoma can appear in the bladder, where it is a less common, non-urothelial type of cancer. Across all these sites, the defining feature of adenocarcinoma is its origin in glandular tissue, which influences its behavior, diagnosis, and treatment.

Cancer Cells are abnormal cells characterized by uncontrolled growth and division, often resulting from genetic mutations or errors. Unlike normal cells, they break the standard rules of cell growth, multiply rapidly, and can avoid the natural process of cell death. These cells can crowd out and damage normal cells, leading to the formation of tumors and causing various symptoms. A defining feature of cancer cells is their ability to spread, or metastasize, to other parts of the body through the bloodstream or the lymphatic system. Lymph nodes can filter out these cells as they travel, which is a key part of how cancer spreads and is detected.

Cancer cells exhibit distinct behaviors that aid in their detection and treatment. They consume sugar at a higher rate than normal cells, causing them to appear as bright spots on PET scans, a common imaging test used for detection. Their rapid growth and spread make them targets for aggressive treatments, such as high-dose chemotherapy, which is designed to kill these dividing cells. The presence and behavior of cancer cells are central to diagnostic procedures, including imaging tests, and to the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at controlling or eliminating them.

In the context of staging, the primary tumor's extent is a key component in determining the overall cancer stage. While the term generally applies to any cancer's starting point, it can specifically describe tumors located in particular anatomical regions, such as a mass formed by cancer cells within the oropharynx or the initial tumor formed in the nasopharynx.

entities.description:
Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an alliance of cancer centers that develops and publishes expert recommendations and guidelines for cancer care. Its primary role is to provide evidence-based treatment guidelines, which are widely used by healthcare professionals to determine appropriate therapies, including chemotherapy regimens. NCCN also offers patient-specific guidelines and resources, making complex medical information accessible to individuals affected by cancer.

In addition to its clinical guidelines, NCCN provides patient education materials, including an app designed to deliver cancer information and assist with managing treatment side effects. The organization also facilitates patient feedback through surveys, which can be accessed via its website at NCCN.org/patients/feedback. These resources aim to support patients in understanding their diagnosis, treatment options, and care pathways, including referrals to specialized cancer centers and genetic counseling for individuals with inherited cancer syndromes.

Overall, NCCN functions as a comprehensive resource hub, bridging expert medical knowledge and patient support. Its dual focus on professional treatment standards and patient empowerment underscores its commitment to improving cancer care quality and patient experience across the continuum of care.

Breast Cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in breast tissue, most commonly originating in the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units, specifically within the ducts or lobules. The vast majority of breast cancers are carcinomas. This malignant disease can spread to surrounding tissue and other parts of the body, such as the lungs; when it metastasizes, it is still referred to as breast cancer.

The condition is frequently associated with germline mutations, particularly in the BRCA genes, and can be hereditary in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. A personal or family history of breast cancer may also be linked to an increased risk of developing other cancers, such as prostate cancer and thyroid cancer. Clinical discussions of breast cancer often focus on staging, prognostic factors, and the use of biomarker testing and tumor markers for diagnosis and management.
