The mouth, or oral cavity, is the first part of the digestive and respiratory (breathing) systems. The lips, cheeks, palate, teeth, and tongue make up the mouth. The mouth helps us breathe, talk, chew, taste, swallow, eat, and drink. The cheeks and lips hold food in the mouth and help to form and sound words. Parts of the mouth The 2 main functions of the mouth are eating and speaking. The mouth is also known as the oral cavity or the buccal cavity. Some important structures of the mouth: Hard palate is the hard, bony part of the roof of the mouth. The mouth Tongue is a muscular organ in your mouth that aids in chewing, speaking, and breathing. Lips surround the opening of the mouth. Buccal (oral) mucosa is the lining inside the cheeks and inside where the lips touch the teeth. Alveolar ridge is the bony, raised area of the upper (maxilla) and lower (mandible) jaw that holds the sockets of the teeth. Gums (gingiva) surround the base of the teeth and help keep them in place. Retromolar trigone is the small area behind the wisdom teeth. Oral mucosa The oral mucosa is the mucous membrane lining the inside of the mouth and lips. It is made up of 2 layers. Epithelium – The surface layer containing stratified squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells. Lamina propria – The bottom layer of connective tissue. A tumor can grow through the layers of the oral mucosa. A measure of how deep the tumor has grown is called depth of invasion (DOI). Depending on the region of the mouth, the epithelium may be nonkeratinized or keratinized. Nonkeratinized squamous epithelium covers the soft palate, inner lips, inner cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and area underneath the tongue. Keratinized squamous epithelium is present on rough surfaces caused by chewing such as the gums (gingiva) and hard palate as well as the top of the tongue. Mouth Cancer, also known as oral cancer or oral cavity cancer, is a malignant condition that develops in any part of the mouth, including the lips, buccal mucosa (inner cheek lining), tongue, gums, floor of the mouth, hard palate, and retromolar trigone. It is classified as a type of head and neck cancer and most commonly originates in the squamous cells, making it typically a squamous cell carcinoma of the mucosa of the lip and other oral surfaces. The disease is a recognized topic in medical literature and is referenced in resources such as the NCCN (National Comprehensive Cancer Network) guidelines, which provide further information on its management.

Clinically, Mouth Cancer is staged using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system, with stages ranging from 0 to 4. This staging process is crucial as it directly guides treatment decisions, helping clinicians determine the appropriate therapeutic approach based on the extent of the disease. However, from a molecular perspective, testing for this cancer has limited value due to the scarcity of targeted drugs available for its treatment, which contrasts with other cancer types where molecular profiling may offer more actionable therapeutic options. Overall, Mouth Cancer encompasses a range of malignancies within the oral cavity, with its diagnosis, staging, and treatment protocols being well-documented in oncological practice.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures of the lymphatic system and integral components of the body’s immune system. Distributed throughout the body, they act as filters for lymph fluid and help fight infection. In the context of cancer, lymph nodes are significant because they can be primary sites of metastasis, where cancer cells spread from a primary tumor. Regional lymph nodes are those located near the tumor, and sentinel lymph nodes are specifically the first nodes to which cancer cells are expected to drain and spread. Cancer involvement in lymph nodes can cause them to swell, and this spread is often detected through imaging techniques such as PET/CT scans, as well as through biopsies. Because they are common sites of metastasis, lymph nodes are frequently biopsied to determine whether cancer has spread, which is a critical step in staging and treatment planning.

Head And Neck Cancer is a broad and diverse category of malignancies that arise in the squamous cells lining the mucosal surfaces of the head and neck region. This group encompasses cancers of the oral cavity (including the mouth, jaw, teeth, and gums), the pharynx (throat), the larynx (voice box), and associated glands. As a broader classification, it includes specific subtypes such as throat cancer. The primary risk factors for developing these cancers include the use of tobacco and alcohol, though a subset of these cancers is also caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).

The disease and its treatment can have significant impacts on a patient's quality of life, potentially affecting the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may necessitate dental work prior to the initiation of treatment. Furthermore, cancer therapies for this region can impact fertility. For patients, particularly those with smoking or vaping habits, cessation is deemed essential to maximize the chances of a cure and to minimize the severity of treatment-related side effects.

Myeloblasts are immature blood cells that originate from myeloid progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Under normal conditions, they are very immature white blood cells that mature into non-lymphoid blood cells, specifically differentiating into granulocytes (such as neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils) or monocytes. As a type of blast cell, they represent an early stage in the myeloid cell lineage.

In pathological contexts, myeloblasts play a central role in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In AML, these immature white blood cells become abnormal and accumulate in the bone marrow and blood, preventing normal blood cell production and function. Similarly, myeloblasts are identified as a type of blast cell involved in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where their presence reflects disrupted myeloid maturation. Across these conditions, the key characteristic of myeloblasts is their immaturity and their failure to undergo normal differentiation, leading to their accumulation and impairment of healthy hematopoiesis.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Histology is the branch of biology and medicine concerned with the study of the microscopic structure of tissues, including their cells and anatomy, as well as the structure of organs under a microscope. In clinical practice, histology involves the detailed review of the appearance and cellular composition of tissue samples. This discipline is fundamental to pathology, where it is used to classify cancer subtypes—such as renal cell carcinoma (RCC)—by examining tissue under a microscope. Additionally, histology is employed to determine tumor grade and assess tumor grade, which informs prognosis and guides treatment decisions. The classification of tumors based on the microscopic appearance of cells and tissues is a core application of histology, making it essential for accurate diagnosis and therapeutic planning.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells found in tissues forming the surface of the skin, mucous membranes, and the lining of various organs and airways. Because these cells are widespread, squamous cell carcinoma can develop in multiple anatomical sites, and its characteristics, prevalence, and staging vary depending on the location.

In the context of lung cancer, squamous cell carcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that originates in the squamous cells lining the bronchi or airways. In the head and neck region, it is the most common type of mouth cancer, arising from the squamous cells lining the mucous membranes inside the mouth, and it is also the most common type of throat cancer, forming in the thin, flat cells of the mucus membranes. For throat cancer, staging information for this type is provided when the tumor tests negative for p16. Additionally, it is the most common type of nasopharyngeal cancer, forming in the squamous cells lining the nasopharynx, and the TNM staging system is specifically applied to this type of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma is also the most common type of cervical cancer, arising from squamous cells in the ectocervix. In the bladder, it represents a less common, non-urothelial type of cancer. Finally, it is the most common type of anal cancer, originating in the squamous cells that form the surface of the skin and other tissues, and it is the focus of certain patient guides for anal cancer. Overall, while the fundamental origin in squamous cells is consistent, the clinical significance, frequency, and management of squamous cell carcinoma are highly dependent on the primary site of the disease.

Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.

Fertility is the ability to conceive or have children, a consideration that applies to individuals of all genders. In the context of cancer care, fertility is a significant health concern because cancer treatments—including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and other modalities—can adversely affect a person’s reproductive capacity. This impact is relevant across various cancer types, such as follicular lymphoma, head and neck cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), and anal cancer, among others.

For patients, fertility is an important topic to discuss with their healthcare team before and during treatment planning. Such discussions allow for proactive measures, including fertility testing for all genders, to assess and preserve reproductive potential. The potential for treatment-related infertility means that fertility considerations should be integrated into the overall care strategy, ensuring patients are informed about risks and available options. Across different cancer diagnoses, the core message remains consistent: cancer treatment may affect fertility, and addressing this concern is a vital part of comprehensive patient care.

Systemic Therapy is a broad category of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to reach and affect cancer cells throughout the body, rather than targeting a single localized area. These therapies are typically administered intravenously or orally, allowing the medicine to travel through the bloodstream to reach cells in any part of the body. This approach is used to treat various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), Ewing sarcoma, metastatic cervical cancer, and bladder cancer, among others. Systemic therapy can be employed as a primary treatment, as an initial therapy, or before or after surgery (neoadjuvant or adjuvant settings), and may also be used as maintenance therapy to prevent recurrence.

The main types of systemic therapy include chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill rapidly dividing cancer cells, while targeted therapy focuses on specific molecules involved in cancer growth, such as HER2-targeted agents or inhibitors. Immunotherapy harnesses the body’s immune system to fight cancer. Other forms include endocrine (hormonal) therapy, which is often used in hormone-sensitive cancers, and platinum-based chemotherapy regimens. These treatments can be used alone or in combination, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Because systemic therapy affects cells throughout the body, it can impact both cancer cells and normal cells, leading to a range of potential side effects. Common short-term side effects include tiredness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, and low blood cell counts. Some side effects may be delayed and occur years after treatment. Additionally, certain systemic therapies, particularly some targeted treatments, can affect fertility. The specific side effects and their severity vary based on the drugs used, the dosage, and the individual patient.

Genetic Testing is a medical diagnostic process that analyzes DNA to identify inherited (germline) mutations, typically performed on normal tissue samples such as blood, saliva, cheek swabs, or urine. This form of testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, as it focuses on determining whether an individual carries hereditary genetic changes that increase their risk for developing cancer. It is commonly used to detect mutations in BRCA genes and other cancer-related genes, and is recommended for all individuals diagnosed with ovarian cancer to guide clinical management.

The scope of genetic testing extends beyond hereditary risk assessment. In oncology, it is also utilized to analyze genetic changes and biomarkers within cancer cells—such as leukemia cells—to inform treatment decisions and prognosis. Additionally, genetic testing serves as a method to identify specific mutations linked to prostate cancer and other malignancies, helping to tailor therapeutic approaches. The test can be performed on various sample types, including blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue, depending on the clinical question.

Genetic testing is also valuable for identifying mutations that cause inherited cancer syndromes, and results are often relevant for family members, as knowing whether a relative has undergone testing can influence interpretation of one’s own results. Overall, genetic testing plays a critical role in cancer risk assessment, early detection, and personalized treatment planning across multiple cancer types.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

The liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts work together to make, store, and secrete bile. Bile is a fluid that helps digest fat in the food you eat. The liver The liver is a large organ located on the right side of the body under the rib cage. Inside the liver is a network of blood and lymph vessels. The liver filters blood, helps with blood clotting, makes bile, breaks down fats, and helps process sugar for energy. The liver also produces lymph. Lymph gives cells water and food and contains white blood cells that fight germs. The liver has two lobes, a right and left lobe. Blood enters the liver from the hepatic artery and the portal vein. Blood leaves the liver through the hepatic veins before entering the inferior vena cava and returning to the heart. Bile is a yellow or green fluid made up of cholesterol, bilirubin, salts such as potassium and sodium, water, and other elements found in the body. It flows into small channels that drain into thin tubes called ducts. These ducts form larger and larger channels that flow into the left and right hepatic ducts. The left and right hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct. The common hepatic duct joins with the cystic duct that connects to the gallbladder to form the common bile duct. It is sometimes described as sac-like because it holds bile from the liver. Ultrasound is a medical imaging technique that uses high-energy or high-frequency sound waves to create pictures of the inside of the body. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. The colon wall is made of layers of tissue. Cancer starts in the innermost layer that comes in contact with food. This layer is called the mucosa. The next layer is the submucosa. It is made of connective tissue and contains mucus glands, blood and lymph vessels, and nerves. The submucosa is followed by a layer of muscle called the muscularis propria. The outer, fourth layer is called serosa (or adventitia). If left untreated, cancer cells grow through the layers of the colon wall, towards the inside of the abdomen. You may notice blood in your stool, on toilet paper, or in the water of the toilet bowl. Anal itching is also common. However, because anal cancer is fairly rare, certain specialists are best qualified to evaluate you. Such specialists include colorectal surgeons and health care providers trained to conduct a test called high-resolution anoscopy (HRA). HRA typically takes place after a digital rectal exam (DRE) is performed. Digital rectal exam The digital rectal exam (DRE) is an important exam for diagnosis, staging, and follow-up. There is nothing high-tech about a DRE. Digit is another word for finger. In a DRE, your doctor inserts a gloved, lubricated finger into your anus and rectum. This finger exam can detect or assess growths or other abnormalities in the anal canal and nearby areas. High-resolution anoscopy (HRA) HRA is a procedure that allows your health care provider to view and examine the anal canal with magnification. A special magnifying glass called a colposcope is then used to closely examine the tissues of the anal canal. The acetic acid makes abnormal cells appear differently when viewed with the colposcope. If abnormal or suspicious areas are seen, a sample of tissue is removed and tested. This is called a biopsy. This biopsy sample may provide the diagnosis of anal cancer. If a colposcope is not used for the procedure, it is simply called standard anoscopy. Colon cancer is a disease characterized by the growth of malignant cells in the colon, a part of the large intestine. It is a distinct form of cancer with treatment approaches that differ from those used for rectal cancer. The disease commonly originates from polyps, particularly adenomatous polyps, which are abnormal growths on the inner lining of the colon that can become cancerous over time. Colon cancer is considered a common and treatable form of cancer, especially when detected early, and it can present in various stages, including stages 1, 2, and 3, as well as in non-metastatic or metastatic forms.

The condition may be linked to family history, suggesting a potential genetic or hereditary component that can increase an individual's risk. Additionally, research indicates that having colon cancer may be associated with an elevated risk of developing prostate cancer. As a disease, colon cancer involves the uncontrolled division of abnormal cells within the colon, and its progression and severity are typically classified by staging systems that help guide prognosis and treatment decisions.
